title: Dirty Secrets of Nuclear Power in an Era of Climate Change
text: Dirty Secrets of Nuclear Power in an Era of Climate Change. This book helps to understand the serious limitations and drawbacks to nuclear power. This is an open access book.

title: A Proposal for Canada to Meet Its Greenhouse Gas Emissions Goals
text: A Proposal for Canada to Meet Its Greenhouse Gas Emissions Goals. Canada is on track to miss the goals of its 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan by a wide margin, which means that it will abrogate its international commitments to reduce its greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in line with the United Nations' global plan to prevent an environmental catastrophe negatively affecting all of humanity. This research examines Canada's policy alternatives and advances a novel plan of action (a new policy framework) that removes partisan politics from emissions-mitigation decisions at the federal, provincial, and territorial levels. The framework establishes independent, technocratic commissions modelled after the institutional independence of central banks, such as the Bank of Canada. Drawing on interviews with climate-policy experts, public administrators, and industry analysts, the study finds that the principal barriers to meeting the country’s emissions goals are not technical but political. The Canadian federal system favours short-termism, making long-term plans that require cross-party support impossible to enact. Participants across ideological lines expressed conditional support for the concept of non-partisan commissions but doubted its political feasibility. When the research concluded in May 2025, participants viewed the recent election of Prime Minister Mark Carney, with experience leading two central banks, as a potential opening for him to champion the plan and facilitate its adoption. At that moment, non-partisan commissions appeared to offer a pragmatic middle course between federal command-and-control and laissez-faire provincialism, and the study identified specific implementation steps that could have supported progress toward Canada’s 2030 emissions goals. However, between then and April 2026, when the dissertation was defended and finalized, the federal government moved in a different direction, weakening key mitigation instruments and narrowing the proposal’s immediate pathway to adoption. An epilogue situates that shift within a broader democratic and historical context and recasts the framework as a proposal to be further refined for a future period of greater public and political receptivity.

title: Essays on financial markets: aquaculture finance, energy transition, and intangible governance
text: Essays on financial markets: aquaculture finance, energy transition, and intangible governance. This doctoral dissertation investigates the pricing, management, and mitigation of risk in modern financial markets, traversing the domains of natural resource economics, energy transition finance, and corporate governance. As the global economy enters an era of polycrisis defined by accelerating climate change, structural policy shifts, and complex agency conflicts, traditional valuation frameworks, which are often predicated on assumptions of linearity, stationarity, and limited dimensions, are increasingly insufficient. This research proposes and validates a unified computational and empirical framework to address these challenges, comprising four independent but thematically integrated essays. The first essay addresses the curse of dimensionality in natural resource valuation by applying Deep Q-Learning to the optimal harvesting problem in aquaculture. Treating the harvesting decision as a real option, the study evaluates Deep Reinforcement Learning as a scalable, nonparametric alternative to regression-based methods such as Least-Squares Monte Carlo. In the baseline setting, the DQN policy produces harvesting times that are broadly comparable with the LSMC benchmark, although the estimated option values remain lower. The main advantage of the framework is therefore its capacity to accommodate richer state spaces without requiring a rapidly expanding set of manually specified basis functions. The second essay bridges biological modeling and financial engineering to value a novel hedging instrument: the biomass futures contract. By integrating a stochastic biological growth model, which accounts for thermal stress, mortality shocks, and growth rates contingent on temperature, with a Schwartz dual factor pricing model, the study quantifies the hedging demand against production risks driven by climate change. The findings reveal that the economic value of biomass futures is highly dependent on the underlying state. These contracts offer substantial downside protection and fundamentally alter optimal harvesting strategies, primarily under scenarios of extreme environmental volatility. The third essay develops a physics-informed real options framework for evaluating nuclear power investment over extended horizons under climate-policy uncertainty. A key innovation is the incorporation of a climate tipping point that introduces a structural break into the natural carbon-decay mechanism and, in turn, the carbon-pricing function. Comparing alternative continuation-value approximators shows that tree-based methods, particularly Random Forest and XGBoost, are well suited to representing non-smooth exercise boundaries and can produce economically meaningful differences at the margin relative to global polynomial smoothing. The model interprets the additional value associated with the anticipated crisis regime as a "fear premium", reflecting ambiguity about a potentially irreversible environmental regime shift before the physical threshold is actually crossed. The fourth essay extends the analysis to corporate finance, examining the role of Organizational Capital as an intangible governance mechanism. Using a comprehensive panel of U.S. firms, the study documents a significant negative association between Organizational Capital and future stock price crash risk. This relation is conditional on the surrounding governance environment and is stronger in several settings characterized by effective monitoring, managerial expertise, and stronger compensation incentives. Together, these essays advance the understanding of how financial agents price and manage complex risks, demonstrating the necessity of integrating advanced computational techniques with contextual physical and organizational insights.
